clue.text: Suspicious about outburst, getting written assurance

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for suspicious is wrapped around the outburst

parts.note: suspicious means wary
a rant is an angry outburst

explanation.surface: Someone wary of a customer's angry outburst insists on getting a guarantee in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' is a link word joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A warranty is a written guarantee given by a seller that goods will perform as promised.

clue.text: Like a candle, it's both good and bad

explanation.surface: A candle is said to be both good and evil at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's both' and 'and' are link words. 'Wicked' is slang praise in Britain meaning excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked means having a wick, as a candle does; in slang it means excellent; and in its normal sense it means evil.

clue.text: Nearly got lift home with fruit

indicators.note: nearly means almost all, so the word for lift loses its last letter

parts.note: to raise is to lift
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone almost managed to get a ride back with some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got' and 'with' are link words; 'Nearly' cuts the final E from RAISE.
explanation.definitionFit: A raisin is a dried grape, a sweet dried fruit.

clue.text: Horrify a friend, embracing copper

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the friend word wraps round the copper symbol

parts.note: a pal is a friend
P is short for penny, a British copper coin

explanation.surface: Shock a friend by hugging a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is P, a penny, which British coins of low value are made from.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal is to shock or dismay someone greatly.

clue.text: Goethe, at realising he holds the stage?

indicators.note: he holds means the phrase contains the answer inside its run of letters

explanation.surface: The German writer is pictured grasping the stage while he takes a role.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'goeTHE AT REalising'. The question mark marks 'the stage' as a definition by association: the theatrical profession.
explanation.definitionFit: The stage is a common metonym for the acting world and playhouses.

clue.text: Science that measures one's spirits

explanation.surface: A branch of science that gauges your mood.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs an optic is the device fixed to an upturned spirits bottle that dispenses a measured shot; the surface reads 'spirits' as mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Optics is the physics of light; optics are also bar dispensers delivering exact measures of gin or whisky.

clue.text: Capital invested in head of school

explanation.surface: Money put into the budget of a headmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal is the sum of money invested before interest, and also the person who runs a school or college.

clue.text: Follows suit — if it is meat stew

indicators.note: a stew mixes ingredients together, so the three words' letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Copying another, someone wonders if it is meat in the stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if' is a link word; 'stew' is the anagram signal, not food.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow suit is to copy what someone else has done.

clue.text: Directions on what to do before catching the mail

definitions.text: Directions on what to do before catching the mail

parts.words: Directions on what to do before catching the mail
parts.note: read as a charade of hints: what you do to a letter before it goes, followed by the mail; the whole is a post bearing directions

explanation.surface: Instructions for what to do before the postal collection.
explanation.walkthrough: You put your name to a letter before posting it, and the whole word is a roadside post giving directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A signpost is a pole carrying arms that show the way to places.

clue.text: Carpenters have steak and kidney, say, smothered in French fries

indicators.note: smothered in means covered over, so the pastry dishes sit inside the fried potatoes

parts.note: French fries are chips
steak and kidney is an example of a type of pie, so this gives pies

explanation.surface: Woodworkers tuck into steak-and-kidney pies buried under a heap of fries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' is a link word. CHIPPIE is British slang for a carpenter (and also for a fish-and-chip shop, which the surface plays on).
explanation.definitionFit: Chippies is informal British slang for joiners and woodworkers.

clue.text: Metal tubes get very hot

explanation.surface: Metal pipes become scorching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' is a link word; 'piping hot' is a set phrase for food served steaming.
explanation.definitionFit: Piping means a length of tubing, and in the phrase piping hot it means steaming, extremely warm.

clue.text: Having nothing to do with the French support for identification

indicators.note: in a down clue, a support goes underneath, so the French article sits below the identification

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: Being unoccupied, and having nothing to do with French identity cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle means unoccupied, inactive, with no work to fill the time.

clue.text: Toiled, ate, worked and became pale

indicators.note: worked suggests being kneaded or shaped, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: After toiling and eating, a labourer turns pale from exhaustion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Etiolated describes a plant grown without light and so blanched, and by extension a person looking weak and wan.

clue.text: Coal, primarily, perhaps Davy's vice

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the opening letter of the word coal

parts.note: the Davy lamp was the miner's safety lamp invented by Humphry Davy, so Davy's thing, perhaps, is a lamp

explanation.surface: A coal-mining puzzle asking whether Davy had a bad habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vice' looks like a moral failing but is the workshop tool that grips things. The Davy lamp was a safety lamp used in British coal mines.
explanation.definitionFit: A clamp, like a vice, is a device that grips and holds work firmly in place.

clue.text: Prohibit English? It's a curse

parts.note: to prohibit is to ban

explanation.surface: Should English be forbidden? That would be a curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bane is a source of persistent trouble or misery, much like a curse.

clue.text: A lock up? I have to be forceful

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for lock is written from bottom to top

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to lock up and decides to be firm about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link word. 'lock' is a curl of hair, not a fastening.
explanation.definitionFit: Assertive means confident and forthright, insisting on one's view.

clue.text: Unknown quantity in English newspapers, say

indicators.note: in places the unknown quantity inside the combination of the other two pieces

parts.note: the press is the collective term for newspapers
in algebra x stands for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A puzzling amount turns up in English newspapers, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' at the end looks like 'for example' but is the definition: to express something is to say it.
explanation.definitionFit: To express a thought is to put it into words, to state it.

clue.text: Prisoner found in strange piles of liquid waste

indicators.note: found in tells us the prisoner word sits inside the jumbled letters
strange signals the letters of piles are rearranged

parts.note: a lag is British slang for a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: A convict is discovered among odd heaps of sewage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link word. 'Prisoner' is the British slang LAG, not an inmate's name; 'strange' makes SPILE from the heaps, which then holds the convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Spillage is liquid that has been spilt and lost.

clue.text: Textile worker's rank

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled fabric
a worker is an ant, the classic worker insect in crosswords

explanation.surface: The status of someone who works in fabrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worker' in crosswords is often an ant or a bee.
explanation.definitionFit: Sergeant is a military and police rank above corporal.

clue.text: Satisfied with rent in the outskirts of pontypridd

indicators.note: in tells us the rental word sits inside the edge letters
the outskirts of a place are its edges, so take the first and last letters of the town name

parts.note: to lease is to rent

explanation.surface: Someone is happy with the rent they pay on the edge of a Welsh town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word. Pontypridd is a town in south Wales; its first and last letters are P and D.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleased means content or gratified, the same as satisfied.

clue.text: Bats died at the back

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies
aft means at the back of a ship

explanation.surface: Bats perished at the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying animals but is the British slang adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats is informal for mad, eccentric; foolish or crazy, just as daft means silly.

clue.text: Daring to have taken a wicket, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word for taking a wicket is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: in cricket a batsman dismissed by the ball hitting the stumps has been bowled

explanation.surface: It takes nerve to claim a wicket in cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bowler who knocks over the stumps has bowled the batsman out.
explanation.definitionFit: Bold means courageous and willing to take risks, as daring does.

clue.text: British birds and dogs

parts.note: eagles are birds of prey

explanation.surface: British birds and dogs listed together like a wildlife survey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Beagles are small scent hounds bred for hunting hares.

clue.text: One's promised to cook in cafe

indicators.note: to cook can mean to fiddle or rearrange, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone has been engaged to work as a chef in a cafe.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiancé is a man engaged to be married, pledged to his partner.

clue.text: The way into extremely small room in church

indicators.note: into means the street abbreviation is put inside the word for extremely

parts.note: very means extremely
St, short for street, is a way

explanation.surface: Directions for squeezing into a tiny chamber in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely small' reads as one phrase, but 'extremely' gives VERY and 'small' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestry is a room in a church where clergy robe and vestments are kept.

clue.text: What to drink — if royal turns up!

indicators.note: turns up, in an across clue, means the word is flipped end to end and read backwards

parts.note: regal means royal

explanation.surface: Deciding on a drink in case a member of the royal family appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if' is a link word; 'turns up' looks like arriving but signals reading the word for royal from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Lager is a light beer, a common choice to drink in a pub.

clue.text: The right to sell ran chiefs ragged

indicators.note: ragged means torn and disordered, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: The bosses were run ragged securing a sales licence.
explanation.definitionFit: A franchise is a licence granted by a company letting someone sell its goods or services.

clue.text: Leader of commons' test for marine growth

indicators.note: leader of means the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: The Leader of the House of Commons faces an exam on sea life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral is a hard reef-building substance formed by tiny sea creatures.

clue.text: A state spies on plant

parts.note: CA is the postal abbreviation for California, a US state
the CIA is the American spy agency

explanation.surface: A US state keeps its agents watching a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link word; 'plant' looks like a factory or a planted agent but is the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The acacia is a tree or shrub, the wattle of Australia, so a kind of vegetation.

clue.text: Wine drinking at home with player of note

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so the wine word swallows the word for at home

parts.note: claret is red Bordeaux wine
in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: A celebrated musician enjoying wine at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word. 'player of note' sounds like a famous performer but is an instrument that plays notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A clarinet is a woodwind instrument, something that plays musical notes.

clue.text: There's a book from it!

indicators.note: from it suggests making something out of the letters given, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a book can be made out of these letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange the six letters of 'There's' to spell a book of the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Esther is one of the books of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Rest, and play around with a mediaeval instrument

indicators.note: around means about in a muddled way, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A minstrel relaxes and fiddles about with an old instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the two fodder words and 'with' is a link word; 'play' is part of the fodder, not the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The psaltery is a plucked stringed instrument of the Middle Ages, like a zither.
